Research code and notebooks on entropic partial Gromov optimal transport (EPGOT)
between Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). Each notebook reproduces figures from the
paper and is published here with its outputs, so the figures on this site are the
ones the code actually produces.

Source: [yachimura-lab/EPGOT-PMGW](https://github.com/yachimura-lab/EPGOT-PMGW).

## The notebooks

| Notebook | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| [Figures 1–3](notebook/figure1_2_3.ipynb) | Transport plans from entropic partial OT between two GMMs, swept over $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ |
| [Figure 4](notebook/figure4.ipynb) | Barycentric interpolation between the same two mixtures, driven by a partial plan |
| [Figure 5](notebook/figure5.ipynb) | Transport maps between sampled point clouds, via barycentric projection |
| [pMGW2 / MGW2 / GW2 / PGW2](notebook/PMGW_corrected.ipynb) | The four matching methods compared on one pair of 3D point clouds |

## Why partial transport

The running example in the first three notebooks is a pair of Gaussian mixtures:
`A`, with two components, and `B`, with two matching components plus a third of
weight $0.1$ parked far away — an outlier.

Balanced optimal transport has to move *all* of A's mass, so that outlier always
receives something. Entropic partial transport prices mass instead, solving

$$
\min_{\gamma \ge 0,\ \gamma \mathbf{1} \le a,\ \gamma^\top \mathbf{1} \le b}
\ \langle \gamma,\ M - 2\lambda \rangle
+ \varepsilon \sum_{ij} \gamma_{ij}\left(\log \gamma_{ij} - 1\right),
$$

where $M$ is the cost between components, $\lambda$ is the reward per unit of
transported mass and $\varepsilon$ is the entropic regularisation strength. Mass
only moves while it pays for itself, so the transported mass
$\sum_{ij} \gamma_{ij}$ can fall below $1$ and the outlier can simply be skipped.

The two knobs pull in different directions, and the sweeps in
[Figures 1–3](notebook/figure1_2_3.ipynb) show it directly: raising $\lambda$ buys
more transport, until the outlier becomes worth reaching after all, while raising
$\varepsilon$ blurs the plan until every pair carries a little mass and nothing is
cleanly excluded.

The same trade-off carries over to Gromov–Wasserstein in
[the point-cloud comparison](notebook/PMGW_corrected.ipynb), where only the
relative geometry of each cloud is available and nothing marks the outlier blob as
spurious.

## Reproducibility

Sampling point clouds and fitting mixtures are both stochastic, so without a fixed
seed every run draws different data and `sklearn`'s `GaussianMixture` converges to
a different local optimum — the figures then change from one run to the next.

Each notebook opens with

```python
from pgot import set_reproducible

set_reproducible()
```

which seeds `pgot`'s generator — along with the global `numpy.random`, `random`
and PyTorch generators — using `DEFAULT_SEED = 42`, and pins `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`
so the timestamp Matplotlib writes into EPS, PDF and SVG files stays fixed.
Re-running a notebook therefore reproduces its figures exactly, rather than merely
producing something like them.

To vary an experiment deliberately, pass a different seed —
`set_reproducible(seed=7)` — or override it per call: the entry points
(`pMGW2_coup`, `MGW2_coup`, `MEW2_coup`, `compute_T_X_to_Z`, …) accept
`random_state` for the mixture fits, and the sampling helpers (`sample_from_gmm`,
`T_rand`, …) accept `rng`.

## Running the code

The logic lives in the `pgot` package under `src/`. `figure4` additionally needs
the compiled `cpp_engine` module, and `PMGW_corrected` needs the vendored
`PGW_Metric` submodule. Dependencies are managed with
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/yachimura-lab/EPGOT-PMGW.git
cd EPGOT-PMGW
uv sync
uv run jupyter lab docs/notebook/
```

Building `cpp_engine` takes a few extra steps — CMake, a C++17 compiler and
Eigen3 — documented in the
[README](https://github.com/yachimura-lab/EPGOT-PMGW#2-build-the-c-computation-engine-cpp_engine).
